Paraklesis
par-AHK-lay-sis
n. (Greek)
Greek paraklēsis, “a calling-alongside,” from parakaleō (to call alongside), from para- (alongside) + kaleō (to call). The semantic range covers exhortation, encouragement, consolation, and (in the noun form paraklētos) advocate, comforter, the Holy Spirit.

📖 Biblical Definition

Paraklēsis is one of the most semantically rich words in the New Testament. The verb parakaleō means literally to call alongside, and the noun paraklēsis names the action of calling-alongside in its several biblical applications: exhortation, encouragement, consolation, comfort. The same root produces paraklētos, the title Christ applies to the Holy Spirit in John 14–16: the Comforter, the Advocate, the One called alongside the believer to teach, witness, convict, comfort, and abide forever. The semantic range is therefore wide, and the same Greek word can do work that English needs three or four words to do. In exhortation: he that exhorteth, on exhortation (Rom 12:8); but exhort one another daily, while it is called To day (Heb 3:13—the verb behind exhort). In encouragement: now the God of patience and consolation grant you to be likeminded one toward another (Rom 15:5); that ye might be comforted together with you by the mutual faith both of you and me (Rom 1:12—paraklēthēnai). In consolation: blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God (2 Cor 1:3-4—the noun paraklēsis and the verb together five times in the verse). In Christ’s naming of the Spirit: and I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever (John 14:16—paraklētos). The biblical pattern is therefore that paraklēsis is the rich Spirit-mediated ministry by which the gospel-truth is brought to bear upon the soul in the precise mode that soul most needs in the moment: as exhortation for the drifting saint, as encouragement for the discouraged, as consolation for the bereaved, as advocacy for the accused. The Spirit Himself is the paraklētos, and the ministry the apostles, the elders, and the saints perform is derivative of His: they call alongside one another with the gospel-truth as the Spirit teaches, applies, and brings home. The category is structural to apostolic ministry. Paul’s epistles are saturated with the verb and noun; his pastoral approach is parakletic (calling-alongside) before it is anything else; the church is to be a community in which the ministry of paraklēsis is mutually exercised by every Spirit-filled saint.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

(Greek term.) Paraklēsis: a calling-alongside; the rich Spirit-mediated ministry by which the gospel-truth is brought to bear upon the soul as exhortation, encouragement, consolation, or advocacy according to the need of the hour. The Holy Spirit is the paraklētos par excellence; saints exercise derivative paraklēsis in the body.

PARAKLESIS — (Greek noun, G3874.) A calling-alongside; exhortation; encouragement; consolation; comfort. The cognate paraklētos (G3875) is Christ’s title for the Holy Spirit (John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7) and is applied to Christ Himself in 1 John 2:1 (we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous).

COMFORTER, n. — One who administers comfort or consolation; one who strengthens and supports under affliction or calamity. The Holy Spirit is so called by Christ. I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter (John 14:16).

📖 Key Scripture

2 Corinthians 1:3-4 — "Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God."

John 14:16 — "And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever."

Romans 12:8 — "Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation: he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness."

Hebrews 3:13 — "But exhort one another daily, while it is called To day; lest any of you be hardened through the deceitfulness of sin."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Paraklēsis is corrupted, in the contemporary church, by the splitting of its rich semantic unity into separated specialties (the exhorter does not console, the consoler does not exhort, the encourager does not call-alongside in any substantive sense)—and by the loss of the Spirit-mediated character of the ministry, treating paraklēsis as a human pastoral skill rather than as the Spirit’s own work through Spirit-filled saints.

expand to see more

The semantic richness of paraklēsis has been split in the contemporary church into separated specialties whose practitioners often do not overlap. The exhorter (the strong preacher who confronts) is a different person from the consoler (the grief-counselor); the encourager (the affirming friend) is a different person from the advocate (the lawyer or pastoral defender). The Greek word and the biblical pattern hold these together: paraklēsis is the rich Spirit-mediated ministry by which the gospel-truth is brought to bear upon the soul in the mode that soul most needs in the moment—exhortation, encouragement, consolation, advocacy—by the same Spirit working through the same called-alongside saint. The recovery is the recovery of integrated parakletic ministry: saints who can call alongside one another with whatever the moment requires, whether that is the hard word of exhortation or the tender word of consolation, and elders who can do the whole work of the gospel ministry rather than only its narrow specialties.

The deeper corruption is the loss of the Spirit-mediated character of the ministry. Christ’s explicit teaching is that the paraklētos par excellence is the Holy Spirit, and that the parakletic ministry the apostles and saints perform is derivative of His. The Spirit calls alongside through them; the truth they bring is applied to the soul by Him; the comfort consoled with is the comfort wherewith they themselves were comforted of God (2 Cor 1:4). Where this Spirit-mediated character is lost, paraklēsis becomes a human pastoral skill—techniques of counseling, practices of encouragement, methods of exhortation—divorced from the dependence on the Spirit’s working that the apostolic pattern requires. Recover both ends. Restore the semantic integration of the rich biblical ministry, and restore the Spirit-mediated character of the ministry. The saint who calls alongside another saint with the gospel-truth, in dependence on the Spirit who is Himself the great Paraklētos, is exercising the very ministry the apostles named—and the church saturated with such mutual parakletic ministry is the church in which the Comforter’s own work is mediated through the body of Christ to every member who is in need.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek paraklēsis (a calling-alongside; exhortation, encouragement, consolation, comfort), cognate with paraklētos (the Comforter, the Holy Spirit—John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7; also of Christ in 1 John 2:1)—the rich Spirit-mediated ministry by which the gospel-truth is brought to bear upon the soul in the mode the moment requires.

expand to see more

Greek paraklēsis (G3874) — exhortation, encouragement, consolation, comfort (29 NT uses).

Greek parakaleō (G3870) — to call alongside; the verb (109 NT uses).

Greek paraklētos (G3875) — the Comforter, Advocate, called-alongside one; Christ’s title for the Holy Spirit (John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7) and applied to Christ Himself (1 John 2:1).

Greek para- + kaleō — alongside + to call (the etymological structure).
